title: First-Round Screen Tips to Win Top Talent (October 2026)
summary: Prep smarter for phone screens with six tips to spot dealbreakers early and win over top candidates. Refreshed for October 2026.
body_markdown:
Nailing the first conversation with a new candidate is critical to meeting your hiring goals. These[first-round screen tips](https://www.dover.com/) exist because, without proper prep work, you lose the chance to attract and inspire top talent to join your team. Most early-stage teams treat the phone screen as a quick filter, but it also shapes how candidates feel about your company before they ever speak to a second person. A rushed or inconsistent screen signals a disorganized process and costs you candidates who had other options. Getting it right from the start matters.


**TLDR:**


-


Build a scorecard covering demeanor, experience, technical fit, and role-specific concerns before your first screen.


-


Asking questions in the same order for every candidate reduces affinity bias and improves how well scores predict job performance.


-


Your pitch should frame the company as a problem/solution statement; candidates are assessing you as much as you are assessing them.


-


AI screening tools are now used by more than half of organizations, making live phone screens a stronger signal for motivation and communication.


-


Candidate misrepresentation is a growing concern, with some data suggesting proxy interviews on virtual calls are no longer rare.


## What a Well-Run Screen Can Do for You


A well-run screen can also help you:


-


Check for potential dealbreakers early on (e.g. availability, relocation, proficiency in your tech stack, etc.)


-


Ask for clarification on information in candidates’ resumes or LinkedIn profiles


-


Assess candidates’ verbal communication skills (in some cases, test candidates for their ability to speak foreign languages)


-


Get to know candidates


-


For passive candidates, learn about their goals and desire to switch companies


Based on thousands of interviews conducted for top startups, we have distilled 6 difference makers to help you decide who you should pass to the next round, and who you should **hard pass** on.


## 1. Do Your Homework


If you sourced a candidate on your own, you may already know why you selected them and which qualifications stick out to you. However, if they’re an inbound applicant, meaning they applied to your job posting directly, look at their LinkedIn profile and resume, making any notes of specific questions you have at this stage.


## 2. Create a Scorecard


A scorecard helps you to remain consistent and fair when assessing candidates. Doing this before beginning your search can help you figure out what you’re actually looking for in the role, and what qualities could instead be “nice-to-have”.


Some areas to consider are:


Scorecard Area What to Assess Red Flags


**General Demeanor** Politeness, timeliness, friendliness, ability to articulate ideas clearly Leaves you with less energy than you started with; poor articulation


**Past Experience / Career Path** Where they see themselves in the next year; ability to explain technical projects simply Goals don’t align with the role; can’t explain complex work in plain terms


**Professional Requirements** Specific programs, tech stack knowledge, and role-specific skills Missing must-have technical proficiencies for the role


**Areas of Concern** Communication skills, availability, start date, role-specific fit (e.g. comfort with company mission) Poor communication, misaligned start date, discomfort with core company context


1.


**General demeanor** : This can include politeness, timeliness, friendliness, and the ability to articulate ideas clearly. Did you leave the interview with more energy than you came in with?


2.


**Past experience or career path:** Where do they see themselves in the next year, and could this role meet those needs and goals? If it’s a technical role, were they able to explain highly technical projects in a clear and simple way?


3.


**Professional requirements you care about** : This can range from experience in specific programs you will need the role to use frequently, tech stack knowledge, or other specifics that pertain to the role.


4.


**Any areas of concern:** Poor communication skills, potential issues in start date/qualifications, etc. This can also be company-specific. For example, one of our top customers HeyJane provides affordable and accessible abortion care. They asked us to assess how comfortable candidates were with using the word “abortion.” Those who seemed hesitant would obviously not be the right fit. If you’re building this out for the first time, our[interview scorecard guide](https://www.dover.com/blog/interview-scorecard-guide) walks through how to weigh areas like this one.


We created a series of scoring rubric templates across the most popular personas startups hire. You can also download a ready-to-use[phone screen scoring rubric](https://www.dover.com/ebooks/phone-screen-scoring-rubric) or, for a deeper look at building one, see our[interview scorecard step-by-step guide](https://www.dover.com/blog/interview-scorecard-guide) .


## 3. Eliminate Bias With an Ordered List of Questions


Studies show that asking questions in the same order for all candidates results in[higher predictive validity](https://www.siop.org/tip-article/is-cognitive-ability-the-best-predictor-of-job-performance-new-research-says-its-time-to-think-again/) on job performance and[lower individual interviewer bias](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9553626/) . In other words, you’re less likely to assess candidates on a “gut feeling” versus their actual response to each question. This tends to point to affinity bias or the idea that we gravitate toward people like ourselves in appearance, beliefs, and background. That’s not to say you shouldn’t be friendly or polite, but if you were more chummy with one candidate over another, it could cloud your perception of who is actually qualified for the role and who you simply enjoyed talking to.


## 4. Perfect Your Pitch


Think of your pitch as a problem/solution statement. What are you doing and why? Why now? You want to anticipate what questions candidates might have so you’re not caught off guard. Include any unique attributes: are you disrupting an outdated industry? Is your software the first-of-its-kind? Do you offer all new hires a free puppy? Mention this in your pitch.


Remember: you’re also being assessed by a candidate while you assess them. For a startup hiring their first employees, a recruiting pitch is your one chance to capture their attention, especially if you don’t yet have a strong employer brand. It also helps candidates to speak to specific role or company pain points during the interview.


**Pro tip: Don’t pitch all candidates the same way.** Consider the type of role you’re hiring for: is it an entry-level position with straightforward responsibilities? You might want to spend more time on a creative pitch, as candidates will likely be more interested on what separates your company from others in the context of this role. On the other hand, if it’s a founding engineer role, you’ll want to perfect your pitch *and* outline a few projects they might work on in the first few months to a year.


## 5. Treat It Like a First Date


Don’t launch into your company’s mission statement the minute a candidate says “hello.” Just as you’re assessing their interpersonal skills, they’re also trying to figure out if they’d like to work with your team. Show up early, be polite, and make them feel welcome by asking about their day or weekend before coming in with your elevator pitch.


During the interview, be an active listener by acknowledging their responses, paraphrasing their answers to show you understand or asking for further clarification.


## 6. Outline Next Steps at the End of the Call


One of the top reasons candidates drop off is if they feel like they have to hound you to set up another time or let them know they’re not moving on to the next stage. If you definitely know you’d like to move forward, schedule the next interview at the end of the phone screen. If it’s clear that you’ll have to reject a candidate, try to do so within the next 1 to 2 days. If you need help constructing a thoughtful rejection email, check out our[rejection email guide](https://www.dover.com/ebooks/rejection-emails) . For more on what happens after a strong screen, see how to get better phone screen to onsite conversion.


After the call, write any final notes in the rubric while they’re still fresh in your mind. Research on[post-interview notes and job performance prediction](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.522830/full) shows that structured note-taking tied to job requirements is a valid predictor of how a candidate will perform on the job.


## What’s Changed in 2026: AI Screening and Candidate Fraud


[SHRM’s 2025 Talent Trends survey](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/2025-talent-trends/ai-in-hr) found that 51% of organizations now use AI for recruiting, up from 26% in 2024. Candidates who reach you have typically cleared at least one automated filter already, so the first live conversation is less about cutting obvious misfits and more about reading genuine motivation and communication quality. Weight demeanor and real-time reasoning more heavily on your scorecard, and open with genuinely open-ended questions rather than prompts that invite a rehearsed answer. Specificity in a response is a stronger signal than a polished pitch that could describe any company.


Candidate misrepresentation has also become a real concern.[Checkr’s 2025 Hiring Hoax survey](https://checkr.com/resources/articles/hiring-hoax-manager-survey-2025) of 3,000 U.S. hiring managers found 35% confirmed a proxy attended a virtual interview in their organization. A few adjustments reduce your exposure: require video for all screens, ask at least one question that requires recalling a specific past decision, and cross-reference a detail or two from their resume in real time. None of these are foolproof, but they raise the cost of misrepresentation enough to surface most cases before a deeper round.

## FAQs


### What should a phone screen actually accomplish?


A phone screen serves two purposes: checking for dealbreakers before investing more time (availability, relocation, compensation expectations, required technical proficiencies) and giving both sides a first read on fit. It’s not a deep skills assessment; that belongs in later rounds. A well-run screen tells you whether a candidate is worth the full interview investment, and it gives the candidate a chance to assess whether your team is worth their time.


### How many questions should I ask, and should they be the same for every candidate?


Research on structured interviewing shows that asking questions in the same order across all candidates produces higher predictive validity and reduces individual bias. In practice, that means building a short, ordered list before you start screening, typically enough to cover general demeanor, relevant experience, professional requirements, and any areas of concern specific to the role. Consistency matters more than volume; a focused set of five to seven questions, asked the same way each time, will tell you more than an improvised conversation.


### What goes on a scorecard for a phone screen?


A useful phone screen scorecard covers four areas: general demeanor (politeness, timeliness, ability to articulate ideas clearly), past experience and career path (where they see themselves in the next year and whether this role can meet those goals), professional requirements specific to the role (tech stack, tools, domain knowledge), and any role- or company-specific concerns (start date, communication style, comfort with the company’s mission). Building the scorecard before you start screening also helps clarify what’s a hard requirement versus a nice-to-have.


## Final Thoughts on Phone Screening That Actually Works


Putting these[first-round screen tips](https://www.dover.com/) into practice consistently saves time, reduces bias, and signals to strong candidates that your process is worth their investment. Build your scorecard before you start, pitch with intention, and follow up within a day or two.
